title: Where does Spain actually live?
text:
NotePhase A — administrative + H3 view



This is the first of two phases. Phase A (here) answers where people live from the census and the map. Phase B adds NASA Black Marble night-lights to validate where inside each municipality they actually live. Built and run on Databricks Free Edition serverless.

title: Where does Spain actually live?
text:
The question
Spain’s population register, the INE Padrón Continuo, is published per municipality — and municipalities are wildly uneven in size. Madrid is one polygon; so is a 12-person hamlet in Soria. Ask “where do people actually live?” with raw municipal data and the map lies: it tells you about administrative borders, not about people.

title: Where does Spain actually live?
text:
The finding
The lie is measurable. Take every Spanish municipality’s population density (people per km², computed on an equal-area projection) for 2022:



Measure
people / km²




Median municipality
13


Mean municipality
180


The average person’s density (population-weighted)
2,508



Half of Spain’s municipalities sit below 13 people/km² — the empty interior, la España vaciada. Yet the typical Spaniard lives at roughly 2,500 people/km². That’s a 14× gap between the average place and the average person. A map coloured by municipality shows you empty land; it does not show you where the country lives.

title: Where does Spain actually live?
section: Four views of the same 47.5 million people
text:
Four views of the same 47.5 million people
The same population, drawn at four different units. Watch how the story sharpens as the spatial unit gets more honest.

By municipality (~8,100 units)



Population density by municipality, 2022




By province (50 units)



Population density by province, 2022




By autonomous community (17 units)



Population density by autonomous community, 2022




On a uniform H3 grid (equal-area hexagons)
The administrative units all share one flaw: they vary in size and shape, so colour partly encodes geography rather than density. Uber H3 replaces them with equal-area hexagons, so colour means one thing everywhere — and the population map and the density map become the same map.



Population density on an H3 grid (res-6), 2022

title: Where does Spain actually live?
text:
How it’s built
A lakehouse pipeline — no GIS server, just Databricks SQL + the native spatial functions:

Join INE Padrón population to IGN municipal boundaries on the 5-digit INE code (8,131 municipalities matched cleanly; the boundary set’s extras are non-municipal territorial entities and disputed enclaves, reconciled to the unit).
Density, honestly — reproject to the ETRS89 / LAEA equal-area CRS (EPSG:3035) and divide population by real km². Density is non-additive, so it’s recomputed (not averaged) at each level when dissolving up to province and CCAA.
H3 allocation — polyfill each municipality to res-9 cells and distribute its population across them, then roll up to res-6 for the national view. Population conserves to 99.998%.

-- Allocate municipal population to H3 cells (native Databricks h3_*),
-- simplifying geometry first so the polyfill stays cheap on detailed boundaries.
SELECT  h3_toparent(cell, 6)                         AS h3_cell,
        SUM(poblacion / num_cells)                   AS poblacion
FROM (
  SELECT  codigo_municipio, poblacion,
          explode(h3_polyfillash3string(ST_AsWKT(ST_Simplify(geometry, 0.001)), 9)) AS cell,
          size(h3_polyfillash3string(ST_AsWKT(ST_Simplify(geometry, 0.001)), 9))     AS num_cells
  FROM    municipios_geo
)
GROUP BY h3_toparent(cell, 6)

title: Where does Spain actually live?
text:
What’s next — Phase B
The H3 map still assumes population is spread evenly within each municipality. It isn’t. Phase B brings in NASA Black Marble (VIIRS) night-lights to reallocate population by how brightly each cell glows — turning “where the register says people are” into “where the lights prove they are.” That’s the validator, and the published thread, still to come.

  About — what Prospectra is
  Prospectra is a geospatial analytics practice, built in public. Spain has a gap: the traditional GIS shops don't run on the lakehouse, and the big Databricks consultancies don't do geospatial. Prospectra is being built to live in that intersection — Databricks-native spatial pipelines on Spain's open data.
  Right now it's week 5 of a six-month sprint: twenty lessons, five portfolio projects, each shipping as a public article. Block 1 of the curriculum is cleared; the first project ships May 26. This site is the stage where the work goes public.
